questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Complex Numbers / Arithmetic, conjugates and equations
questions.stem: Let $z=3-5i$. The imaginary part of $\bar{z}$ is
questions.solution:
Conjugating keeps the real part and reverses the sign of the imaginary part:
$$\bar{z}=3+5i.$$

The imaginary part is the coefficient of $i$, written without the $i$. Here that coefficient is
$$5.$$
distractorRationale: Gave the imaginary part of $z$ itself. Conjugating flips that sign, so the answer must change sign too.
Gave the real part. Conjugating leaves it alone, but it is not what was asked for.
Correct. $\bar{z}=3+5i$, whose imaginary part is $5$.
Flipped the sign of the real part instead of the imaginary part.

questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Complex Numbers / Arithmetic, conjugates and equations
questions.stem: Let $z=(2+3i)(1-i)$. The real part of $z$ is
questions.solution:
Expand the product term by term:
$$(2+3i)(1-i)=2-2i+3i-3i^{2}.$$

Now use $i^{2}=-1$, which turns $-3i^{2}$ into $+3$:
$$=2+3+(-2+3)i=5+i.$$

So the real part is $5$ and the imaginary part is $1$.
distractorRationale: Correct. $-3i^{2}=+3$, so the real part is $2+3=5$.
Used $i^{2}=+1$, which turns the last term into $-3$ and gives $2-3$.
Gave the imaginary part instead. The question asks for the real part.
Multiplied the two real parts only, $2\times 1$, and never expanded the bracket.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Complex Numbers / Arithmetic, conjugates and equations
questions.stem: Solve $(1+i)z=3-i$. The imaginary part of $z$ is
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — isolate $z$.**
$$z=\frac{3-i}{1+i}.$$

**Step 2 — clear the denominator.** Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate $1-i$, which turns the bottom into $1^{2}+1^{2}=2$:
$$z=\frac{(3-i)(1-i)}{2}.$$

**Step 3 — multiply out.** Remember $i^{2}=-1$:
$$(3-i)(1-i)=3-3i-i+i^{2}=3-4i-1=2-4i.$$

**Step 4 — divide through.**
$$z=\frac{2-4i}{2}=1-2i.$$

The imaginary part is the coefficient of $i$, taken with its sign and without the $i$ itself, so it is $-2$.
distractorRationale: Multiplied by $1+i$ rather than by the conjugate $1-i$, which flips the sign of the answer.
Gave the real part of $z$ instead of the imaginary part.
Expanded the numerator correctly but never divided by $|1+i|^{2}=2$.
Correct. $z=\dfrac{2-4i}{2}=1-2i$, whose imaginary part is $-2$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Complex Numbers / Modulus and the complex plane
questions.solution:
The modulus is the distance from the origin to the point $(-8,\ 6)$ in the complex plane, so Pythagoras applies:
$$|-8+6i|=\sqrt{(-8)^{2}+6^{2}}.$$

The squares kill the minus sign:
$$=\sqrt{64+36}=\sqrt{100}=10.$$
distractorRationale: Added the two parts as they stand, $-8+6$, and took the size of the result. Distance needs squares, not a plain sum.
Correct. $\sqrt{64+36}=10$.
Added the sizes of the two parts, $8+6$. That would be the journey along the axes, not the straight-line distance.
Stopped at $64+36$ and never took the square root.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Complex Numbers / Modulus and the complex plane
questions.solution:
There is no need to carry out the division. The modulus of a quotient is the quotient of the moduli:
$$|z|=\frac{|5+5i|}{|3-4i|}.$$

**Step 1 — the top.** $|5+5i|=\sqrt{25+25}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt{2}$.

**Step 2 — the bottom.** $|3-4i|=\sqrt{9+16}=5$.

**Step 3 — divide.**
$$|z|=\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{5}=\sqrt{2}.$$
distractorRationale: Correct. $\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{5}=\sqrt{2}$.
Reported $|z|^{2}=2$, stopping one step before the square root.
Divided by $|3-4i|^{2}=25$ rather than by $|3-4i|=5$ — the denominator was squared twice.
Took the modulus of the numerator only, leaving the denominator out.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-3 / Geometry and Algebra / Complex Numbers / Modulus and the complex plane
questions.stem: Every complex number $z$ with $|z-3|=|z+1|$ shares one real part. What is it?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — read the two moduli as distances.** $|z-3|$ is the distance from the point $z$ to the point $3$, and $|z+1|=|z-(-1)|$ is its distance to $-1$.

**Step 2 — name the locus.** The points equidistant from two fixed points form the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. Both fixed points lie on the real axis, so the bisector is the vertical line through their midpoint.

**Step 3 — find the midpoint.**
$$\frac{3+(-1)}{2}=1.$$

So every such $z$ has real part $1$. Writing $z=x+yi$ confirms it: $(x-3)^{2}+y^{2}=(x+1)^{2}+y^{2}$ collapses to $-6x+9=2x+1$, giving $x=1$ for every $y$.
distractorRationale: Reported the fixed point $-1$ itself rather than the midpoint of the two fixed points.
Read $|z+1|$ as the distance to $+1$, which makes the midpoint $\dfrac{3+1}{2}=2$. The sign inside the modulus reverses.
Reported the other fixed point, $3$, rather than the midpoint.
Correct. The locus is the perpendicular bisector of $-1$ and $3$, the vertical line $x=1$.
